episode_thesis: Dunne and Kaastrup-Larsen (Systematic Investor 313, recorded mid-September 2024) argue that the post-2022 regime is one of higher macro and rates volatility: a data-dependent Fed starting an easing cycle toward an uncertain neutral rate, a possible further inflation surge (Rogoff), a fragile decades-long carry regime that depends on trust in central banks, and leverage structures that turn volatility spikes into deleveraging (the August 2024 yen carry unwind). On the investing side they argue, via Asness's paper, that uncorrelated high-volatility alternatives such as trend following are capital-efficient (cheap futures leverage, portfolio-level Sharpe, zero not negative equity correlation) and that institutions over-prefer low-volatility products for governance and behavioural reasons.

speakers.name: Alan Dunne
speakers.role: Co-host; macro and CTA analyst, rules-based investor commentary
speakers.speaker_note: Transcript captions spell the name 'Alan Don'; ledger spelling 'Alan Dunne' kept. Turn attribution is clear from the host handing over topics. Much of the second half is Dunne relaying Asness's papers, Rogoff's interview, the BIS paper and Posen: those are third-party arguments he endorses or qualifies, flagged as such where relevant.

worldview_premises.premise: The theme of Jackson Hole each year reveals what policymakers think is the dominant macro problem (supply constraints 2022, debt 2023, transmission of hikes 2024), so it is a read on the policy regime.
worldview_premises.support: Year-by-year recall of Jackson Hole themes.

worldview_premises.premise: Inflation will be higher and more volatile than before 2020 because periodic supply shifts will recur and central banks will tolerate inflation rather than unemployment, so disinflation should not be extrapolated as a permanent solution.
worldview_premises.support: Endorses Rogoff (Harvard): political support for fighting inflation is thin; Rogoff forecasts another 2021-22-type surge within 7-8 years. Dunne concedes falling CPI/PPI give ammunition to the opposite view.

worldview_premises.premise: A Fed that has shifted from forecast-based to data-dependent policy reacts quickly to each weak release, so interest-rate volatility around data and political events rises.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from the stated reaction function (a -100k payrolls print would force a 50bp cut); no data cited.

worldview_premises.premise: Policy stance is not summarised by the policy rate: long yields, equities and credit spreads set financial conditions, so policy can be loose while the rate is called restrictive; the neutral rate itself is unobservable in real time.
worldview_premises.support: Powell's 2018 point that r-star cannot be estimated in real time; Adam Posen conversation (financial conditions matter more than the policy rate, and excessive central-bank communication is a problem).

worldview_premises.premise: Neutral is drifting up (long-run dot 2.5% to about 2.8%) because the real-neutral assumption has risen on productivity and fiscal expansion, and a 2.5-3.5% range still leaves much easing room versus a 5-5.25% policy rate.
worldview_premises.support: Fed Summary of Economic Projections long-run dot; 0.5% real neutral plus 2% inflation construction.

worldview_premises.premise: Low volatility invites leverage (lower margin requirements) and a volatility spike forces deleveraging and degrossing through higher margins, margin calls and vol-adjusting participants; the structure that produced August 2024 is still there.
worldview_premises.support: BIS paper on the August 2024 turbulence and the yen carry unwind; BIS own conclusion that dysfunction was averted but the structure deserves attention.

worldview_premises.premise: Perceived market stress now exceeds arithmetic moves because markets are monitored in real time and by social media; the August 2024 S&P fall was about half October 1997 yet produced calls for emergency cuts.
worldview_premises.support: Personal recollection of trading in London in 1997; Jeremy Siegel's call for 75bp cuts as the contrast.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following has roughly zero correlation to equities, not negative, so periods when both lose are normal and do not make it an unreliable diversifier; in deleveraging events bonds rally, but in inflation-driven episodes like 2022 bonds and trend can fall together.
worldview_premises.support: Definition of zero correlation; Einstein 'as simple as possible but not simpler' on the 'zig when equities zag' slogan; TLT +10% since July as the August example.

worldview_premises.premise: Faster information has not made markets more efficient (value spreads stay wide even adjusting for tech); the wisdom-of-crowds argument needs independent participants, and common information and social media may reduce independence. Dunne flags that the herding half of Asness's argument is qualitative and a hypothesis.
worldview_premises.support: Asness paper on value spreads in 1999-2000 and 2019 relative to history; no data for the herding argument.

worldview_premises.premise: At the portfolio level volatility drags compound returns, but a high-volatility component that is uncorrelated with the rest can add value even with periodic total losses, so component volatility should be judged by its contribution to the whole, not on its own.
worldview_premises.support: Asness's arithmetic: 66%/33% bet example and mean-variance optimizer results under assumed correlations (alts 0 to equities, bonds 0.3); Dunne notes the result depends on those assumptions.

worldview_premises.premise: High-volatility futures funds are the cheapest and most available leverage (priced near overnight rates versus a 2-4% bank spread), so a 25% vol alternative lets the investor hold a smaller weight and add bonds, improving diversification and Sharpe.
worldview_premises.support: Asness paper plus Dunne's own argument about bank margin spreads; no numerical backtest quoted.

worldview_premises.premise: Institutions prefer 8-10% vol products while family offices accept 20%, probably because boards and committees dislike explaining large drawdowns; behavioural resistance and the first 3-6 months after allocation are the main obstacle.
worldview_premises.support: Own experience with allocators; Asness anecdote that AQR's first offering was high-vol and immediately drew down.

worldview_premises.premise: Multi-manager hedge-fund flows reversed (first outflow in seven years, about $30bn) because an earlier one-off rebalancing out of private markets is exhausted, performance disappointed, and pass-through fees (up to about 10% of allocation) and opaque portfolios weaken loyalty once returns slow.
worldview_premises.support: FT report of a Goldman Sachs report; a Mercer hedge-fund research head interview; one allocator conversation.

worldview_premises.premise: European growth weakness is structural (ageing, sluggish productivity, reversal of the post-Schroeder tailwinds of productivity, Eastern outsourcing and cheap Russian energy); pan-European spending only works for cross-border energy and joint defence procurement, and national agendas have always constrained delivery.
worldview_premises.support: Draghi report figures (800bn euros a year, 4.5% of GDP, double the Marshall Plan per the FT); historical recall.

steps.from: Inflation falling toward target
steps.to: Fed no longer needs to be restrictive; Powell signals an easing cycle, not just one cut
steps.why: Waller and Williams echo that the aim is to remove restrictiveness and move toward neutral.

steps.from: Unobservable neutral (about 2.5-3.5%) versus policy at 5-5.25%
steps.to: Market prices about 100bp of cuts by year end and about 3% by mid-next year
steps.why: That equals a move to neutral plus some probability of recession-driven cuts below neutral.

steps.from: Policy calibrated to each data release instead of a 1-2 year forecast
steps.to: A very weak payrolls print forces an immediate 50bp cut; any significant weak data gets an immediate reaction
steps.why: The Fed has said it is data-dependent, which removes the forecast anchor.

steps.from: Reactive Fed plus political risk (a Trump win would extend tax cuts)
steps.to: More rates volatility and market jitters
steps.why: Heavy data-dependence combined with election risk makes the priced easing path unsafe.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Fed projections, Powell/Waller/Williams statements, market pricing; history of 25bp openers in 2001 and 2007.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Dunne says the market path looks fair given neutral estimates; the chain fails if data stay benign and the Fed glides to neutral (he sees 'a lot priced in'). Also he concedes the 25 versus 50 opener is a close call.

mechanism_chains.topic: Low volatility to leverage to deleveraging (August 2024 carry unwind)

steps.from: Extended period of low volatility and Fed put conditioning
steps.to: Low margin requirements and high leverage, including yen carry
steps.why: Cheap leverage is rationally taken when volatility is low.

steps.from: Volatility spike (Nikkei and VIX extremes)
steps.to: Exchange margin hikes, margin calls and vol-adjusted position cuts force degrossing
steps.why: Three mechanical channels named by the BIS.

steps.from: Japanese holders hedge US assets once the dollar-yen trend turns
steps.to: Additional yen buying beyond the visible CFTC position
steps.why: Tactical hedging adds to the yen move and makes the unwind size hard to measure.

steps.from: Trend followers short yen and long equities
steps.to: They help the yen rise only by covering shorts, and are hurt by the V-shaped rebound through position cuts
steps.why: Vol-driven position-size cuts mattered more than the change of direction.

steps.from: Bond rally in the deleveraging
steps.to: TLT about +10% since July, supporting the diversifier role
steps.why: Capital-markets deleveraging events favour bonds; inflation-driven ones (2022) do not.

mechanism_chains.evidence: BIS paper; CFTC data; TLT performance; comparison with October 1997.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Dunne says it is not guaranteed to stay benign: the BIS says dysfunction was averted this time and the same leverage structure could generate a more serious episode.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why a high-volatility uncorrelated alternative improves the portfolio (Asness)

steps.from: Component has high volatility but zero correlation to equities
steps.to: Small weight delivers the same risk contribution; losses are rebalanced against the rest
steps.why: Portfolio volatility drag applies to the total, not to each component.

steps.from: Optimizer given 10% vol target and zero-correlated alts
steps.to: Allocates to alts instead of bonds (stock-bond-only solution is near 60/40)
steps.why: Result depends on the assumed correlations (alts 0, bonds 0.3).

steps.from: Alternative at 25% instead of 10% vol
steps.to: Smaller allocation, room for bonds, better Sharpe and return per unit of risk
steps.why: Capital efficiency of the high-vol vehicle.

steps.from: Futures fund trades larger positions
steps.to: Investor obtains leverage priced near overnight rate, rather than bank spread of 2-4%
steps.why: Futures embed cheap financing; banks may refuse to lend against a 60/40.

steps.from: Individuals and family offices cannot easily run managed accounts (tax reporting of components)
steps.to: Pooled high-vol funds are the practical route
steps.why: Operational complexity.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Asness's simulations under stated expected-return and correlation assumptions; Dunne notes assumptions could be debated.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If the alternative's equity correlation is not near zero, or the investor abandons it during early drawdowns (transition risk in the first 3-6 months).

mechanism_chains.topic: Why institutions choose low-volatility products and how that is changing

steps.from: Boards and investment committees must explain large drawdowns
steps.to: Institutions request 8-10% vol products
steps.why: Explaining -15% is harder than -5%, even though they know the maths.

steps.from: Zero interest rates
steps.to: Institutions wanted low-vol CTAs with 5-6% returns
steps.why: No interest income meant returns had to come from the strategy alone.

steps.from: Higher interest rates
steps.to: Alpha unchanged, interest income adds to return, more interest in higher-return (higher-vol) versions
steps.why: Returns of the vehicle rise with cash rates.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Kaastrup-Larsen's own product range; Dunne sees US shift beginning.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: UCITS VaR limits cap vol around 15-16% regardless of demand.

decision_process.practice: When building an alternatives sleeve, prefer a 20%-vol uncorrelated strategy at a smaller weight, and add bonds with the capital saved; do not just ask for 'half the amount' of a diversifier.
decision_process.why: Better Sharpe and capital efficiency; 'give me half' arguments do not persuade investors.

decision_process.practice: Use pooled high-volatility futures funds for individuals and family offices; managed accounts for institutions.
decision_process.why: Tax and infrastructure complexity of managed accounts.

decision_process.practice: Obtain leverage through futures rather than borrowing against a 60/40 portfolio.
decision_process.why: Priced near the overnight rate, not 2-4% over; banks may refuse.

decision_process.practice: Read primary papers (Asness, BIS, Draghi report, Rogoff interview) and flag which parts are quantitative and which are qualitative hypotheses, noting the assumptions that drive optimizer results.
decision_process.why: Distinguishes evidence from opinion (herding claim has no data; optimizer result depends on correlations).

decision_process.practice: Trend-following manager speed determines who wins at reversals: fast managers gain when a reversal persists, slow managers when it reverses again.
decision_process.why: Observed dispersion in Dec-Jan and summer 2024; ETF trend products were slower into long bonds.

decision_process.practice: Trend portfolios cut positions after a volatility spike (volatility-adjusted sizing), which can matter more than a direction change in V-shaped recoveries.
Read policy through the destination of rates and overall financial conditions, not just the size of the next cut (25 vs 50bp); Dunne's call was 25bp because the Fed starts cycles at 25bp.
decision_process.why: History of 2001/2007 and the unobservable neutral.

current_views.reasoning: Reactive policy plus election outcome roughly 50/50.

Multi-manager outflows may be the start of a sentiment shift for a crowded strategy; the flow driver may be exhausted.
current_views.reasoning: One-off private-market rebalancing complete, fees, opacity.

current_views.view: The August 2024 stress was concentrated in Japan and volatility products; the panic around the S&P was disproportionate.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host of Top Traders Unplugged; veteran CTA hedge fund manager (CTA industry since 1990)
speakers.speaker_note: His own firm's products (a 20%+ vol version, a half-leverage version, a UCITS fund) are mentioned: bias toward high-vol CTA products should be noted. Two claims corrected per ledger (C16-3 includes speculation he labelled 'facetious'; C17-2 UCITS vol).

worldview_premises.premise: The multi-decade carry regime rests on trust in central bank independence and forward guidance that suppressed volatility; losing independence (political control of the Fed) could trigger bond vigilantes and end the regime.
worldview_premises.support: Links Rogoff's concern about independence to the Rise of Carry book (Kevin Coldiron interview); timing correlation of forward guidance with the extreme carry regime.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors, officials and central banks have been conditioned over 20 years by the Fed put to react to modest drawdowns from all-time highs as emergencies; carry trades will always exist because of Japanese monetary policy, so unwinds recur.
worldview_premises.support: Own career spanning pre- and post-Fed put eras; S&P went about 350 days without a 2% daily drop.

worldview_premises.premise: Labour bargaining power has swung back toward workers (shrinking labour force, behavioural change), a structural source of wage and inflation pressure.
worldview_premises.support: Anecdotes from company managers and a friend; contrast with the 1970s and 1980s union era.

worldview_premises.premise: EU-level initiatives lose energy and money to bureaucracy, so a large European programme may not deliver.
worldview_premises.support: Danish vantage point; no data; he says he does not follow the European economy closely.

worldview_premises.premise: Institutions say they want low fees and transparency but allocate to expensive, opaque multi-managers and private equity: convenience over principle; market-neutral multi-strats harvest small inefficiencies with high leverage that works in a stable carry regime and may suffer when regime or volatility changes.
worldview_premises.support: Personal reasoning; links to carry-regime discussion; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Sharpe was invented for portfolios, not single strategies; maximum drawdown relative to volatility is more informative, and some volatile CTAs have much smaller drawdowns than their volatility suggests.
worldview_premises.support: Assertion from industry experience.

worldview_premises.premise: CTA volatility fell from 20-25% in 1990 (industry under $10bn) to lower levels after institutionalisation from 2000 because committees prefer smaller drawdowns, and possibly because lower leverage lets managers run more capital (his own tongue-in-cheek speculation).
worldview_premises.support: Own career; AUM figures with the Bridgewater caveat (about $150bn of the quoted $400bn).

worldview_premises.premise: Alpha is unchanged when rates rise and interest income accrues directly to the investor, so higher rates raise appetite for higher-return, higher-vol CTA versions; UCITS VaR limits cap vol around 15-16%.
worldview_premises.support: Own product experience; regulation.

worldview_premises.premise: Combining traditional assets with a non-correlated return stream such as trend following gives a safer, higher-returning portfolio; he asserts no white paper contradicts this.
worldview_premises.support: Assertion of the literature without citation.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Asness's herding/independence argument is acknowledged by Dunne to be qualitative with no supporting data, yet used as support for trend and value persistence.

The optimizer result (alts preferred to bonds) depends on assumed zero equity correlation and 0.3 stock-bond correlation, which Dunne notes could be debated; the 2022 experience (bonds and trend falling together) is in tension with a stable zero-correlation assumption.
Kaastrup-Larsen asserts that no white paper contradicts the benefit of adding trend following, without citation, and is a manager promoting high-vol CTA products (conflict of interest).

Claim that Sharpe is meaningless for a single strategy sits uneasily with the same speakers using Sharpe improvement as the evidence for high-vol alternatives (portfolio-level framing resolves it only if correlations hold).
Forward-guidance-to-carry-regime link is a timing correlation, not tested causation; the host himself says he is only connecting dots.
Rogoff's 7-8 year forecast of another inflation surge is a single academic forecast; Dunne notes disinflation data currently point the other way.
Multi-manager outflow causes (one-off rebalancing from privates) come from one allocator conversation and a Mercer view; no flow data beyond the Goldman figure.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs the speakers treat as leading: Fed communications and the next data prints (payrolls) for the pace of easing; long-run dot and long-term yields as neutral and financial-conditions measures; the US election outcome (fiscal path); CPI and PPI surprises for the inflation regime; volatility regime and margin changes (VIX, margin requirements) for leverage/deleveraging risk; CFTC yen positioning plus hedging flows for carry; central bank independence signals for the carry regime; interest-rate level for demand for high-vol CTA products. Horizons are weeks to months for rates, 7-8 years for the Rogoff inflation view.
reader_inferences: (reader) The two speakers see CTAs and trend following as the logical beneficiaries of a world with higher rates volatility and carry-regime fragility, so many macro views serve the thesis that trend is a useful diversifier.

(reader) Dunne's reasoning style is mechanism-then-priced-in: state the policy reaction function, then ask what the market already discounts; Kaastrup-Larsen's is regime narrative from career experience.
(reader) The carry-regime-fragility thesis and the data-dependent-Fed volatility thesis are linked but distinct: the first is about trust in central banks, the second about reaction function.

(reader) The high-volatility argument is partly a capital-efficiency (cheap futures leverage) argument that holds only if investors can hold through early drawdowns; the behavioural obstacle is the main binding constraint, not the arithmetic.
